title: Capacitor-first DRAM: anneal the dielectric before transistors exist
idea: Inverts 'transistor first, capacitor last'. Etch and fill the storage-capacitor array into a bare carrier wafer, anneal the dielectric at 800-1000 C to crystallize ultra-high-k phases (rutile TiO2, SrTiO3, k 80-150) that a finished transistor could never survive, then Smart-Cut-transfer a thin single-crystal Si film on top and build access transistors aligned to the buried capacitor marks.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): k~100 lets pillar AR fall from ~70:1 to ~35:1, removing the slowest high-AR etch/fill steps and their tool count; ~10-15% fewer process hours per wafer.

title: Grow capacitor pillars upward instead of etching 70:1 holes
idea: Inverts 'deep features are carved top-down'. Pattern only a thin hard mask of seed openings, then grow single-crystal Si or TiN-clad nanopillars upward by selective-area epitaxy/CVD to 2-3 um (AR >100:1) and wrap them with ALD dielectric and plate; height becomes a growth-time knob instead of a plasma-selectivity limit.
why: Removes the deepest, slowest plasma etch and its bowing/twisting yield loss (facts 1, 4); AR ~115 reached with no extra litho, ~25% more charge per cell.

title: Relax overlay budgets, ship imperfect arrays, remap at boot
idea: Inverts 'memory must leave the fab perfect'. Loosen the storage-node-to-landing-pad overlay spec ~2x so scanners use fewer alignment marks and rework drops; each 512-row subarray carries ~6% spare columns plus a tiny CAM that the controller fills at power-on from a self-test, remapping bad cells at 64-bit granularity like a flash translation layer.
why: Litho time and rework sit inside the ~55% depreciation share (fact 4); ~15-25% more wafers per scanner-hour for ~6% area overhead.

title: Twin landing pads let EUV expose at half dose
idea: Inverts 'one printed feature per electrical function'. Give every storage node two parallel, slightly offset contact/landing-pad features so a stochastic missing or bridged print of one is electrically harmless, then expose those stochastics-limited layers at ~50% EUV dose.
why: EUV throughput is dose-limited; halving dose on 2-3 of the 5-7 EUV layers raises scanner wafers/hour ~40-60% (fact 4) for a few-to-10% cell-area cost.

title: Never dice: wafer-scale DRAM sold as one memory slab
idea: Inverts 'memory is sold as small diced dies'. Stitch reticles across a full 300 mm wafer, route around dead reticle fields with a wafer-level mesh of fuse-configured links, skip dicing, packaging and per-die test, and ship the whole wafer as a rack CXL memory slab (~3 TB) with optical edge I/O.
why: Eliminates scribe/kerf (~5-8% area), packaging, per-die test and the HBM TSV tax (fact 6); back-end cost per bit -20-30% for pooled capacity tiers.

title: Universal pre-patterned array blanks bought like SOI wafers
idea: Inverts 'every DRAM maker patterns its own array front end'. One mega-line with EUV makes standardized 'array blanks' (honeycomb active area plus buried wordlines, the first ~20 critical steps) for all customers; DRAM makers buy blanks like SOI wafers and finish capacitors, periphery and BEOL on DUV-only lines.
why: Concentrates the 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4) in one fully loaded line, so the rest of industry needs no EUV; scale and utilization could cut litho capital per bit ~30%.

title: One universal grating reticle prints every array layer
idea: Inverts 'each layer needs its own critical mask'. Lay out all array layers (active, wordline, bitline, storage node) on a single gridded honeycomb lattice so one ultra-high-quality periodic reticle prints the dense lines for every layer by rotation/offset, and only coarse DUV-printable cut/keep masks are layer-specific.
why: ~60-70% fewer critical reticles and qualification cycles, and a path to replace 3-4 EUV layers with DUV cut layers (fact 4).

title: Reuse each Czochralski wafer ten times via porous-silicon lift-off
idea: Inverts 'the silicon substrate is consumed'. Anodize a double-layer porous Si film on a prime wafer, grow 2-5 um device-quality epi on it, build the DRAM array, bond to a cheap carrier and split at the porous layer; the prime wafer is repolished and reused ~10x (ELTRAN-style).
why: Cuts prime-wafer demand 5-10x and with it the Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz crucible chokepoint; also hands bonding flows a ready backside.

title: DRAM on glass: repurpose idle Gen-10.5 display fabs
idea: Inverts 'memory needs a semiconductor fab'. Run 2.9 x 3.4 m display lines to build 8 sequential tiers of low-leakage oxide-TFT 1T1C cells at ~1 um rules, giving ~0.5 TB of slow-tier DRAM-class memory per panel for CXL far memory.
why: A Gen-10.5 panel has ~120x a 300 mm wafer's area on built, under-used capital; competitive per GB only if 8-tier panel cost stays under ~$1,500, so it is a capacity-tier hedge with near-zero new fab capital (fact 4).

title: Wafers stay put; process heads travel like print heads
idea: Inverts 'wafers travel between tools'. Clamp each wafer once on a precision carrier for its whole front end; spatial-ALD, atmospheric-plasma etch and DUV/imprint heads sweep over a moving row of carriers like a printing press, so chucking, alignment reference and load-lock overhead are paid once.
why: Removes ~30-40% of non-productive tool time (pump-down, transfer, re-chuck, re-align) and most automated material handling; ~20% less capital per wafer start (fact 4).

title: Vacuum-railway fab with no ballroom cleanroom
idea: Inverts 'a fab is a giant cleanroom building'. Link cluster tools with sealed sub-mTorr maglev tube conveyors so wafers never touch air from bare wafer to passivation; the building becomes an ordinary industrial shed with local maintenance enclosures.
why: Cleanroom shell, make-up air and HVAC are ~20-30% of a $15B fab and a large energy/water load; also removes queue-time oxidation limits.

title: Turn spare 28-65 nm logic fabs into memory fabs
idea: Inverts 'DRAM must come from DRAM fabs'. Standardize a pure-logic-process 3T gain-cell macro (no capacitor module) with on-die short-interval refresh, sold as CXL/UCIe memory chiplets that any mature-node logic fab can run on its existing flow.
why: Unlocks depreciated capacity in months, not 3-5 years; ~0.1-0.15 Gb/mm2 at 28 nm (~3x less dense) on wafers costing ~1/3, near parity cost per bit for cache/near-memory roles.

title: Ionogel double-layer capacitors replace 70:1 dielectric pillars
idea: Inverts 'the storage dielectric is a solid insulator'. Fill shallow cups with a confined solid-polymer ionogel so charge sits in a nanometre electric double layer (~20-40 uF/cm2 vs ~7 for ZrO2), meeting 5 fF at AR ~15:1, with blocking electrodes to suppress Faradaic leakage.
why: Removes the hardest high-AR etch and ALD fill (fact 1) with 3-5x charge per area; must prove ns-scale ion response in sub-10 nm confinement.

title: Test storage nodes mid-flow through a sacrificial wiring layer
idea: Inverts 'electrical test happens at the end'. Right after capacitor formation, deposit a temporary metal grid that ties storage nodes into addressable test groups, map shorts and leakers with a probe card in minutes, strip it, and feed the map to redundancy planning and scrap/rework before the costly BEOL.
why: Stops spending ~40% of remaining process cost on doomed wafers and cuts yield-learning loops from ~3 months to ~1 (fact 4 capital efficiency).

title: One free-electron laser feeds a whole fab of scanners
idea: Inverts 'every scanner carries its own plasma light source'. Build a ~10 kW energy-recovery-linac FEL in the fab basement and split its EUV beam to 8-12 source-less scanners.
why: The source is ~a third of scanner cost and the throughput limiter; ~3x power per scanner allows higher dose (fewer stochastics) or ~2x throughput (fact 4).

title: Bond a sense amp under every 64 cells; shrink capacitors
idea: Inverts 'bitlines must be long and capacitive'. Hybrid-bond a sense-amp wafer under the array at ~250 nm pitch so each local bitline serves only ~64 cells, cutting bitline capacitance from ~60 fF to ~8 fF; the cell then needs only ~1-1.5 fF, a stubby AR ~10:1 capacitor.
why: Breaks the charge wall (fact 1) by changing the transfer ratio, not the charge; removes the deepest etch, ~4 masks and much of the fill tool set.

title: Print the array once; later layers grow onto it
idea: Inverts 'each layer is lithographically re-registered'. One EUV exposure defines the honeycomb of active pillars; wordline recess, storage-node contact, landing pad and capacitor are then built on it by area-selective ALD, selective epitaxy and spacer self-alignment, so the pattern is inherited rather than re-printed.
why: Removes 3-5 of the 5-7 EUV layers and their overlay budgets (fact 4); ~20-30% lower litho capex per wafer.

title: Flip the wafer: build capacitors on the backside
idea: Inverts 'capacitors sit above bitlines on the front'. After front-side transistors and bitlines, bond to a carrier, thin to ~0.5 um and open storage-node contacts from the back directly onto source/drain, building capacitors over the full cell footprint with no bitlines in the way.
why: Removes the buried-contact and landing-pad layers that snake past bitlines (1-2 EUV layers) and gives ~1.5x capacitor footprint, so AR can drop ~30% (facts 1, 4).

title: Helium-free plasma tools: hydrogen backside gas, textured chucks
idea: Inverts 'etch and deposition chucks need helium backside cooling'. Use low-pressure H2 or H2/Ne backside gas (thermal conductivity ~1.2x He) with a micro-textured AlN chuck face and closed-loop recapture of all purge gas.
why: Helium is a live chokepoint (Qatar offline since March 2026); substitution plus recapture could cut fab helium use >90% at low capex.

title: Treat DRAM fabs like dams: 30-year public depreciation
idea: Inverts 'fab capital must be repaid in five years'. A public infrastructure authority owns shell, utilities and long-lived tools (furnaces, wet benches, CMP), depreciated over 25-30 years, and leases capacity at cost to memory makers who own only the short-life leading-edge tools.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (fact 4); moving ~half of capex to 30-year life cuts wafer cost ~20-25% and speeds U.S. siting.

title: Hyperscalers consign their own tools inside memory fabs
idea: Inverts 'the fab owns its capital'. A cloud buyer purchases a block of scanners and etchers, consigns them into a memory maker's line, and receives that block's output at cash cost plus a tolling fee, as in chemical tolling.
why: Moves ~$2-5B of capex per block off the memory maker's balance sheet, lowering its cost of capital and letting capacity start with demand rather than after it.

title: Urban-mining line requalifies retired server DRAM
idea: Inverts 'new supply needs new wafers'. Robotic hot-air reflow strips DRAM packages from retired server DIMMs, a 48-hour retention and row-hammer stress screen sorts them, and they are re-mounted on CXL memory-expander cards for pooled tiers.
why: Hundreds of millions of GB retire yearly; recovered supply at ~10-20% of new-wafer capital per GB, zero EUV.

title: Crucible-free silicon via cold-crucible induction Czochralski
idea: Inverts 'silicon crystals grow from quartz crucibles'. Melt Si in a segmented water-cooled copper crucible where electromagnetic pressure and a solid Si skull keep the melt off the walls, and pull 300 mm crystals with no high-purity quartz.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine >80% quartz chokepoint; lower oxygen content may also tighten the retention tail (fact 3).

title: Superlattice cleave-edge master stamps sub-20 nm DRAM lines
idea: Inverts 'line pitch comes from optics'. Grow a Si/SiGe or GaAs/AlGaAs superlattice by 1990s MBE, cleave and selectively etch its edge into a nanoimprint master whose line pitch equals layer thickness (~16-20 nm), then thermally imprint wordline/bitline gratings with a 1995-style imprint press, using a >=180 nm stepper only for coarse layers.
why: Sub-20 nm dense lines with zero EUV/ArF (fact 4); master replication makes a dense layer cost a few dollars.

title: Crystal planes do the etching: KOH slot capacitors
idea: Inverts 'high-aspect-ratio etch needs plasma tools'. In (110) silicon, KOH/TMAH wet etching stops on vertical {111} planes, giving atomically smooth slots >100:1 deep from stepper-defined (spacer-narrowed) openings; lined with dielectric they form deep slot capacitors that share walls between neighbouring cells.
why: Hits AR ~115 (fact 1) on a ~$200k wet bench instead of $5M+ etchers; density still needs sub-litho line pitch from a companion trick.

title: Deposition sets density: 128-tier DRAM strings from 180 nm holes
idea: Inverts 'density comes from lithography'. Deposit 128 alternating oxide/poly (or Si/SiGe) tiers, punch 180 nm channel holes with a KrF stepper and 1990s deep-trench RIE (AR ~36:1), and form one ring-gate transistor plus lateral-recess capacitor per tier per hole, with staircase contacts made by repeated resist-trim etching.
why: Each 0.13 um2 hole holds 128 cells, ~1,000 nm2 per bit versus ~860 nm2 for a 6F2 cell at 12 nm, with no EUV; capital moves to cheap deposition tools (facts 2, 4).

title: Sixteen-fold spacer multiplication on a 1990s KrF stepper
idea: Inverts 'resolution belongs to the scanner'. Print 360 nm-pitch lines on a KrF stepper and run four rounds of sidewall-spacer transfer (LPCVD nitride/oxide spacers plus RIE), each halving pitch, to reach ~22 nm-pitch array lines with no overlay-critical steps.
why: Modern array pitch from fully depreciated litho; ~5-10x lower litho capex per dense layer (fact 4); line-edge roughness and cut layers are the limiters.

title: Two-terminal DRAM cells at crossings of spacer gratings
idea: Inverts 'every cell needs a three-terminal access transistor'. Stack a vertical n+/p-/n+ punch-through selector on a planar MIM capacitor at each crossing of two orthogonal spacer-defined gratings; the selector conducts only above ~1.5 V, so half-select biasing reads and writes a 4F2 cell with no per-cell gate or contact.
why: Per-cell patterning collapses to two self-aligned line layers, 4F2 from 1990s tools; selector sub-threshold leakage sets refresh (fact 3) and is the risk.

title: Anodized-alumina pores as a ready-made capacitor forest
idea: Inverts 'storage nodes must be individually patterned'. Anodize sputtered aluminium in oxalic acid so it self-orders into hexagonal pores (~25-60 nm pitch, AR >100:1); a 180 nm stepper only fences cell groups, and atomic-layer-epitaxy reactors of the 1990s TFEL-display type line the pores with electrode/dielectric/electrode, several pores in parallel per cell.
why: Self-assembled high-AR template from an electrochemistry bath; ~30x capacitor area per footprint so a 180 nm-rule cell gets ample Cs in a thin layer (fact 1).

title: Catalytic gold-mesh wet etching drills 200:1 nanoholes
idea: Inverts 'deep holes require plasma'. Metal-assisted chemical etching: a perforated Au film (stepper-defined then spacer-shrunk) sinks into Si in HF/H2O2, drilling straight pores or freeing pillars at AR 100-200:1 at room temperature, then the Au is stripped in iodide before any thermal step.
why: Replaces the most expensive high-AR dry etchers (facts 1, 4) with wet benches, with no bowing; serves capacitor holes or vertical-channel pillars.

title: Self-rolling strained films make Swiss-roll capacitors
idea: Inverts 'capacitors are etched into the substrate'. Pattern a strained bilayer (SiNx stressor plus metal/dielectric/metal) at 1 um rules on a sacrificial layer; on release it rolls into a 10-20-turn tube that multiplies plate area per footprint ~20x, then the rolls are anchored and planarized as a capacitor tier.
why: Capacitance from planar 1990s deposition and litho with no high-AR etch (fact 1); rolled-up micro-capacitors exist, per-cell density and contacting are the risk.

title: Thermally drawn fibers shrink a macro-preform into memory
idea: Inverts 'small features need lithography'. Machine a centimetre-scale preform with interleaved metal, glass and semiconductor channels laid out as a capacitor-plus-channel array, then draw it in a fiber tower (~10,000x cross-section reduction) to 50-100 nm features over kilometres; slice into chiplets and stack.
why: Litho-free nanoscale features from 1970s-90s fiber towers; extreme capital efficiency if channel crystal quality and contacts can be solved.

title: Colloidal sphere monolayers print the DRAM honeycomb
idea: Inverts 'patterns must be printed'. Langmuir-transfer a monolayer of 40 nm silica spheres; they self-pack into the same hexagonal lattice DRAM capacitors use, are shrunk by O2/CF4 RIE and serve as the etch mask, while 180 nm stepper fences force grain boundaries onto dummy rows.
why: Sub-50 nm honeycomb with no EUV (fact 4); remaining grain defects absorbed by spare rows.

title: Block copolymer turns 180 nm trenches into 12 nm lines
idea: Inverts 'every line must be exposed'. Spin PS-b-PMMA into 180 nm stepper-defined trenches (graphoepitaxy), anneal so it self-assembles into ~12 nm lamellae aligned to the walls, remove the PMMA and transfer by RIE, a ~15x pitch multiplication from a hot plate.
why: Bitline/wordline gratings at modern pitch with 1990s steppers; materials cost cents per wafer (fact 4).

title: Lensless interference lithography with 1990s excimer lasers
idea: Inverts 'lithography needs a lens and a mask'. Interfere two or three line-narrowed 248/193 nm excimer beams (Lloyd's-mirror geometry) at the wafer to expose ~110-130 nm-pitch gratings or hexagonal arrays over a whole 200 mm wafer in one flash, then halve with one spacer step.
why: A ~$1M optical bench replaces a $100M+ scanner for every periodic array layer (fact 4); coherence over full-wafer area is the risk.

title: Dewetted metal nano-islands roughen electrodes into area
idea: Inverts 'the capacitor needs an ordered geometry'. Anneal a 5 nm sacrificial Sn film so it dewets into ~15-25 nm random islands, use them as an RIE mask to texture the poly-Si storage node into nanopillars (the 1990s hemispherical-grain trick taken ~10x further), strip, then coat with dielectric.
why: 5-10x electrode area per footprint from a furnace and an etcher (fact 1), letting thin planar-ish 180 nm-rule caps hold >20 fF.

title: Fab federation chains depreciated 200 mm fabs into one line
idea: Inverts 'a DRAM line must be one site'. Assign each step block (front end, capacitor, BEOL, test) to one of a dozen fully depreciated U.S. 150/200 mm fabs, move wafers in sealed nitrogen-purged pods on scheduled trucks, and run one shared MES and yield database across them.
why: Uses capital already paid for (near-zero depreciation vs ~55% of wafer cost, fact 4); capacity in 12-18 months; U.S. manufacturability.

title: Half-billion-dollar DRAM line from scavenged 200 mm tools
idea: Inverts 'a memory fab costs $15B'. A consortium buys decommissioned steppers, LPCVD furnaces, RIE and CMP tools at ~3-10% of new price, refurbishes them for a single tier-stacked DRAM flow needing only >=180 nm litho, and replicates the line as identical $0.5B modules.
why: Capital per wafer start ~20-30x lower; profitable even at lower density when tier count supplies the bits (fact 4).

title: Short-loop CCD memory: charge shifts instead of transistors
idea: Inverts 'each bit needs its own access transistor and contact'. Store bits as charge packets in 64-stage recirculating CCD loops with spacer-defined overlapping poly gates; a loop is randomly addressed and streamed out in ~64 x 1 ns, and recirculation doubles as refresh.
why: No cell contacts, capacitor module or leakage-tail access transistors (facts 1, 3); ~2F2 per bit at spacer-defined gate pitch from 180 nm litho; latency is loop-length-bound.

title: Revive the 1990s BST bet: planar k~250 capacitors
idea: Inverts 'more charge needs taller capacitors'. Deposit (Ba,Sr)TiO3 by MOCVD or sol-gel on Pt/Ru electrodes, the material of the 1990s Gbit-DRAM programs, with compositional grading to cut leakage; at k ~250 a 44 nm planar film stores 5 fF in 0.1 um2.
why: Takes fact 1's k~70 escape route with ~3x margin and no high-AR etch, using only 1990s deposition tools.

title: Self-limiting oxidation carves 10 nm channels from 180 nm lines
idea: Inverts 'channel width is printed'. Pattern 180 nm Si lines and use stress-retarded thermal oxidation, which self-limits as the core shrinks, to thin them to uniform ~10 nm wires in a 1990s furnace; strip and wrap with gate for gate-all-around access transistors.
why: Thin all-around channels tighten the leakage tail (fact 3) and cut refresh; sub-litho channels from a furnace, though cell pitch stays litho-bound.

title: Open-hardware 1990s stepper cloned by U.S. machine shops
idea: Inverts 'litho tools come from two or three vendors'. Publish an open design for a 248 nm, 0.6 NA, 5x-reduction stepper (expired patents, catalog excimer lasers, fused-silica lenses ground by U.S. optics shops) buildable for ~$2-3M each in volume.
why: Removes the scanner chokepoint for every non-critical layer and for spacer/BCP pitch-multiplied flows; creates a domestic tool base.

title: Federal offtake guarantees for old-tool tier-stacked DRAM
idea: Inverts 'markets fund only leading-edge memory'. DoD/DOE sign 10-year take-or-pay contracts at a fixed $/GB for DRAM-class memory made on >=180 nm tool lines in the U.S., with the price ratcheting down as tier counts rise.
why: De-risks capital for old-tool high-tier flows and secures defense/critical-infrastructure supply.

title: Fusion-bond stacks of sixteen thinned 180 nm array layers
idea: Inverts 'one wafer makes one memory layer'. Build cheap 180 nm array layers on 200 mm SOI, then oxide-fusion-bond and etch back 16 of them (the 1990s BESOI technique), connected by 2 um through-oxide vias at mat edges to a single bottom periphery layer.
why: ~16x density per footprint with no litho shrink; each layer costs depreciated-tool prices (facts 2, 4).

title: Four-level cells read by time-to-threshold sensing
idea: Inverts 'a DRAM cell stores one binary bit'. Store four charge levels per large 180 nm-rule cell (~30 fF) and read by timing how long the bitline takes to cross a reference, with a ramp and counter shared per mat and reference cells rewritten each refresh to cancel leakage drift.
why: Doubles bits per mask step at fixed litho; big old-node capacitors give MLC the margin modern 5 fF cells lack (facts 1, 4).

title: Laser-grown single-grain silicon tiers stacked over finished arrays
idea: Inverts 'access transistors must live in the wafer'. Deposit a-Si over the previous tier, etch 180 nm grain-filter holes, and melt it with a 1990s XeCl excimer pulse so each transistor sits in one location-controlled grain (micro-Czochralski), then repeat for 8-16 tiers below a 450 C substrate budget.
why: Monolithic 3D without bonding or epi, with one cheap mask set reused per tier (facts 2, 4); grain-boundary-free channels keep leakage near bulk.
